newsitem.title: HUNGARY: World Bank official urges Central Europe reforms.
newsitem.headline: World Bank official urges Central Europe reforms.

text.p: The countries of Central and Eastern Europe should press ahead with modernising their financial sectors to be ready for joining the European Union (EU) by 2002-2003, a World Bank official said on Tuesday.

"Our assessment is that all of these countries are well under way to prepare themselves for EU accession," said Michel Noel, the World Bank's chief of country operations in Central Europe. "But there are certain areas which require special attention."

In a lecture at the Central European University, Noel spoke about the development of the financial sectors of Slovenia, Hungary, Slovakia, Poland and the Czech Republic since they began building market economies.
The financial sectors of those countries presented a mixed picture and there were no clear front-runners among them, he said.
The countries in the region had some common problems, such as less-developed capital markets, weak banking supervision and too much state involvement in the banking sector, Noel said.
Noel said banking supervisors in the region had the appropriate regulatory background but the quality of their operations needed to improve to meet the standards of a market economy.
"That's the key number one challenge in these countries." he told Reuters.
"The second challenge is in particular with the development of the capital markets," he said.
Low turnovers on capital markets in the region have hampered equity and debt financing and the development of emerging enterprises, he said.

"In this area the single most important decision that these countries could make is to reform their pension systems so that private pension funds would flourish and become prime actors to deepen the capital markets," he said.
Noel said all the countries of the region should press ahead with the privatisation of banks to prepare their economies for entering the EU.
He said large state-owned banks in the Czech and the Slovak republics probably need strategic partners to help them continue restructuring.
Poland should also privatise some of its large specialised banks, and Slovenia's largest bank, Ljubjanska Banka, was nearly ready for privatisation, too, he said.
Hungary went a long way toward the privatisation of its banks during the past 18 months, and it should finish what it began, Noel added.

The World Bank official said the insurance sector of the region was less prepared for EU membership than the banking sector. Competition was limited, with a relatively small number of insurance companies operating in each country.
